QF.id: XIII Introduction to Forwards and Futures_55

question.text: What is the impact of 'negative carry' versus 'inverse carry' on bond futures pricing?

answer.text: Futures price = cash price + financing cost − income on cash position; when income exceeds financing cost (inverse carry), bond futures can trade below the spot/fair clean price, while financing greater than income increases the carry cost so the futures premium rises
Negative carry means the futures price is always negative
Negative carry only applies to commodity futures with high storage costs
A scenario where income exceeds financing always pushes the futures price above spot

explanation.text: The Logic: Series IV (pages 126-127) gives the bond-futures pricing relationship as futures price = cash price + financing cost − income on cash position. If financing cost > income, the fair futures price rises above spot (carry cost is positive); if income > financing cost, an "inverse" carry arises and the fair futures price falls below the spot/fair clean price (a discount). The Trap: Futures prices are not literally negative. The label "negative carry" in bond markets refers to the sign of the carry component, not the price itself, and the inverse-carry case (income greater than financing) is what produces a futures discount to spot. Note: Source-backed by Series IV Interest Rate Derivatives workbook, pages 126-127.
